The Pre-Session Warm-Up

Amir Ardekanian · 7 min read · June 2026

📲This article is also in the appAA Performance · opens without an accountOpen →

Here's something most tennis players do before every session: they jog one lap, stretch their legs, hold it for a bit, then pick up their racket.

It feels like warming up. But it's not really helping them. In fact, the stretching part might actually be making them slower.

Here's what actually works — and why.

Why warming up matters

When muscles are cold, they can't fire fast. They're sluggish. The first step is late. The serve feels stiff. Reactions are slow.

When you warm up properly, muscle temperature goes up — and that literally makes muscles move faster. For every degree muscles warm up, explosive power goes up by about 3–4%. Faster serves, quicker feet, sharper reactions.

But here's the catch: the effect doesn't last long. If players warm up and then stand around for an hour, they're basically cold again. Time the warm-up so it ends close to when the session starts — right before, not 30 minutes before.

The one thing to cut

Static stretching before training. Those long holds where players bend down and count to 30 — research is very clear on this: it slows them down. It makes muscles too loose, too floppy, and that actually hurts sprint speed and serve power.

Dynamic stretching — moving through range instead of holding it — gives the same flexibility benefit without the speed cost. Cut the held stretches. Move instead.

The 4-step structure

Step 1 — Raise (3–5 min)

Get the blood moving and the muscles warm. Low-effort movement — players are not working hard yet, just waking up. Jog easy, side shuffles, high knees, butt kicks. Think of it like warming up a car engine — you don't floor it straight away.

Step 2 — Activate & Mobilise (7–10 min)

Move the joints through the ranges tennis actually needs. Leg swings, hip circles, walking lunges with a twist, arm swings, trunk rotations. No holding — keep it flowing. Research on tennis players showed a dynamic warm-up like this made serve speed 4% faster and sprint times 4% quicker compared to a static warm-up.

Step 3 — Potentiate (3–5 min)

Right before the session starts — not 10 minutes before, right before — run 2–3 short maximal sprints (10–15 metres), do a set of sharp jumps (countermovement jumps or ankle pogos), and for players who serve, press the hitting arm hard against a wall for 5 seconds twice. This fires up the nervous system and spikes muscle power just before it's needed. In a study on real tennis players, a potentiation protocol before serving improved serve speed by 4.6 km/h. Keep this under 5 minutes and go straight into the session.

Step 4 — Start immediately

The warm-up keeps players ready for about 30 minutes. After 60, it's mostly gone. Don't let them stand around after it. If there's a long break mid-session, run a quick 2-minute re-raise before going hard again.

At a glance

  • Raise — easy jogging, shuffles, high knees (3–5 min)
  • Activate & Mobilise — leg swings, arm swings, walking lunges, trunk rotations (7–10 min)
  • Potentiate — 2–3 × 10m sprints, 2 × 3 jumps, arm press × 2 (3–5 min, right before starting)
  • Start — do not wait around

The rule

Rule

Move, don't hold. Everything in the warm-up should be moving. If players are standing still counting seconds, it's wrong before a session. Static stretches are for after training — when they're warm, the session is done, and you want to cool down and loosen up. Before training: move. After training: hold.
